analytic.title: Fur and faeces: an experimental assessment of non-invasive DNA sampling for the European pine marten 1

div.p: Non-invasive genetic sampling using materials such as faeces or hair can be used to monitor wildlife 16 populations, although DNA quality is often poor. Improving sampling efficiency and minimising factors that 17 reduce DNA quality are therefore critical. After a severe decline, European pine marten, Martes martes, has 18 reclaimed much of its former range in Scotland, UK. Recording this rapid range expansion requires developing 19 techniques for accurate monitoring, but this is hampered by the species' elusive behaviour. We tested two 20 sampling methods, hair collected from hair tubes and faeces (scat) collected along tracks, to assess the effects of 21 key environmental and sampling variables on DNA quality and sampling efficiency. For hair, we tested the 22 influence of hair tube location (distance from forest tracks) on collection rate and sex ratio of animals 23 successfully sampled. For scats, we assessed the effect of time since defecation (1 to 16 days) on genotyping 24 error rates and success under two contrasting environmental conditions (exposed to rainfall or sheltered). We 25 found no bias in the collection rate or sex ratio of animals detected by hair samples with differing proximity to 26 forest tracks. DNA amplification failure for scats exposed to rainfall increased from 28% to 65% over the 16 27 day experimental period. During periods of low rainfall, the length of collection sessions could therefore be 28 extended to increase sample number without risk of DNA degradation. Lack of bias in hair collection rates with 29 proximity to forest tracks provides justification for tube placement close to tracks, as this reduces survey effort.
These findings provide guidance for the development of efficient and cost effective non-invasive sampling of 31 Scottish pine martens.

Accurate baseline data on species presence, abundance and demographic rates is a key component of effective 37 wildlife management (Gibbs et al. 1999). For rare or threatened species, knowledge of population status enables techniques (Taberlet et al. 1996). Improving the efficiency of sampling and minimising the factors that reduce 65 DNA quality are therefore critical when designing a cost effective surveying strategy.

Despite previous findings that suggest a decrease in faecal DNA quality over time (Brinkman et al. 2010; 67 Panasci et al. 2011), and with increased rainfall (Nsubuga et al. 2004;Murphy et al. 2007;Brinkman et al. 68 2010), there is considerable variation in the effect of these factors between taxa. For example, rainfall 69 significantly degrades DNA in Sitka black-tailed deer pellets (Odocoileus hemionus sitkensis), but does not 70 affect DNA sample quality from mountain gorilla faeces (Beringei beringei; Nsubuga et al. 2004). Similarly, 71 amplification success as faecal samples aged (up to one month) decreased by 65% for the brush-tailed rock- 2011). Genotyping success has been higher for hair samples than scats for pine martens in previous studies 74 (Mullins et al. 2007), but success rates for hair can still vary, with factors such as the number of hairs that are 75 used in the extraction process having a significant effect, as seen for the Asiatic black bear (Ursus tibetanus, 76 Uno et al. 2012), although it remains unclear if differences exist between species.

Pine marten populations in Scotland have shown a recent range expansion after near-extinction in the early 20th 78 century (Lockie 1964;Croose et al. 2013). As a protected native species, there is strong stakeholder interest in 79 the conservation of pine martens, particularly since the suggestion that they may play a role in controlling the 80 invasive American grey squirrel (Sciurus carolinensis; Sheehy et al; 2014). There is concern, however, about 81 the effect of pine martens on vulnerable prey species through, for example, nest predation of capercaillie (Tetrao

Sampling regimes used to estimate population abundance and density should account for differences in 89 detectability, either through sampling design or through statistical methods. For studies using non-invasive hair 90 sampling, time constraints usually make it unfeasible to relocate hair tubes between sampling sessions, which 91 may introduce a temporal bias and violate assumptions of sampling independence (Boulanger et al. 2006). For 92 example, heterogeneity in the probability of capture between individual pine marten has been observed in an

Irish study, with hair tubes placed in lowland forests collecting more samples than those in upland forests, 94 despite similar population densities in both habitats (Lynch et al. 2006). Spatial biases can also occur; hair tubes 95 are most accessible if placed close to forest tracks; pine marten scats are also collected from forest tracks due to 96 the relative ease of collection compared to searching the densely vegetated, forest floor. If some individuals use 97 forest tracks less frequently than others, the samples collected may only represent a sub-set of the population.

Female pine martens, for instance, are thought to be more risk averse than males due to the reporting of a higher 99 proportion of male road casualties (Rob Coope, pers. comm.); females also maintain smaller home ranges than 100 males (Caryl et al. 2012b), which therefore could be less likely to contain forest tracks. As a consequence, the 101 effect of different sampling techniques and designs on the outcome of non-invasive hair sampling is currently 102 unclear.

In this paper we assess the effects of key environmental and sampling variables on the quality of pine marten 104 DNA sampled non-invasively through hair and scats (with the latter divided into experimental treatments to test 105 for the effect of exposure to rainfall), and examine the implications for developing efficient sampling protocols.

div.p: Darnaway was excluded from all analyses due to lack of hair samples. Visitation rate to hair tubes was analysed 190 using a Generalised Linear Mixed effects Model (GLMM) with a binomial error distribution. The response 191 variable was recorded as 'visit' or 'no visit' for each hair tube, replicated per session. To allow us to specifically 192 test the effect of time on the rate of visitation, we included session as a proxy for time elapsed as a fixed 193 covariate, as well as distance (question 1). Forest was included as a fixed factor and two way interaction terms 194 between distance and forests, and distance and session were included (question 2). Hair tube ID was included as 195 a random factor. To test the effect of these variables on the sex-ratio of visitors, the same analysis was used, but 196 with the proportion of males as the response variable restricting analyses to samples with a positive sex ID only 197 (question 2).

To determine whether PCR success for pine marten sex-typing is affected by the number of hair follicles used in 199 the extraction process, we calculated the mean Ct value per sample over positive rtPCR replicates. As the ZFX 200 region is present in male and female pine martens and a Ct value is only obtained for positive samples, we 201 included positive amplifications using the MMX locus only. There are, however, two copies of the ZFX region 202 in female DNA for every one copy in male DNA, so it may take fewer cycles to obtain the threshold level of 203 DNA template for female samples than for males; the effect of this bias should, however, be negligible as Ct
value is unlikely to be reduced by more than one for females as compared to males. A Generalised Linear Model
(GLM) with poisson error distribution was used with Ct value as the response variable and number of hairs as 206 the explanatory variable (question 3).

The effects of time and exposure to rainfall on error rates (allelic drop out, false alleles and failure) were 216 analysed using three GLMMs with a binomial (logit) distribution using proportional data from two repeated 217 amplifications per sample for each combination of treatment, time and locus (question 4). As treatment 218 commenced on day two, samples from day zero were not subject to the treatment conditions and so were not 219 included in the models. Only successful samples (i.e. those that produced DNA) were included in the models for 220 false alleles and allelic drop out. Treatment (exposed, sheltered) and locus were included as fixed factors, time

The amount of amplifiable DNA obtained from hair samples is significantly increased by including more hair 278 follicles in each reaction. Previous studies suggest that one hair is sufficient for accurate genotyping (Higuchi et 279 al. 1988). Our analysis, however, suggests that including more follicles (up to 13) reduces PCR failure rates.

Where funding, or time, prevent processing of all samples, researchers should favour samples with the most 281 follicles to increase PCR success. However, as hair tubes do not prevent visitation by more than one animal per 282 session, the risk that including more than one hair per reaction may produce erroneous genotypes (i.e. via 283 contamination from the second visitor) must be considered. During a larger scale study of pine marten 284 population density in Scotland, including 136 -320 hair-tube nights per forest, no erroneous genotypes were 285 detected (Kubasiewicz et al, Unpublished data). We cannot rule out the possibility that more than one individual 286 was present in a sample, with different homozygous genotypes at one or more loci (i.e. this would present as a 287 heterozygous genotypes which we would not recognise as erroneous). However, as pine martens are attracted to 288 hair tubes with bait, which is removed once a visit has occurred, the chance of multiple visits is low.

There was a significant difference in DNA quality and amplification success between the two loci tested. During 301 initial planning of a project, we would recommend testing a range of potential microsatellite loci for relative 302 success and error rates so that the most effective panel can be chosen. This should be considered as essential as 303 optimising sample collection and storage conditions in developing an efficient and cost effective process.

For scat collection, researchers must strike a balance between leaving sufficient time for samples to accumulate 305 and collecting samples before DNA degrades, particularly during periods of rainfall. If longer sampling sessions 306 are required where populations are thought to be at low density, genotyping success may be improved by 307 sampling during drier periods. For hair, samples are usually collected from stationary sources such as hair tubes.

As such, the time between sampling sessions must also take into account sample independence. For pine 309 martens in Scotland, our data suggest that sessions of longer than four days are required to achieve this

Hair tube visitation rates increased over time with, on 262 average, 2.6x as many samples collected in the fourth session compared to the first. This increase supports 263 previous findings in Ireland, where sampling success increased with time when hair tubes were checked every 264 four to six weeks for six months (O'Mahony et al. 2012). The shorter time period of the current study means that 265 this effect is not due to increased population density, but suggests the influence of two factors; an increase in the 266 likelihood of different animals locating hair tubes over time; and the habituation of individual pine martens to 267 particular hair tubes. The latter of these factors is less apparent as, of 15 identified individuals that made 268 multiple visits during the study period, only one individual used a single hair tube for all of their visits 269 (Kubasiewicz et al. Unpublished data).

Both time since defecation and the level of exposure affected DNA amplification, reinforcing previous findings 290 of the importance of these factors. An increase in PCR failure occurred with time up to 16 days after deposition, 291 but only for scats that were exposed to rainfall. Although this effect was also seen for false alleles, allelic drop 292 out did not increase significantly with time or treatment. As only a small number of repeat amplifications were 293 performed, the increased failure rate over time could have masked any decrease in quality i.e. fewer successful 294 amplifications were available for errors to occur in. Nevertheless, our results highlight the interacting effects of 295 time and rainfall on pine marten scats and we would encourage other studies to assess the drivers of DNA 296 degradation in faecal samples from other mammals. The finding that PCR failure increases with time for scats 297 exposed to rainfall, as opposed to error rates alone, indicates that studies which require identification only at the 298 species level, as well as those requiring accurate individual identification, need to minimise the effect of these 299 factors for ensure a cost and time effective strategy.

Scat samples, however, are difficult to genotype due 312 to high levels of genotyping error associated with the poor quality DNA recovered (Lucchini et al. 2002). It may 313 be beneficial for future studies to evaluate the use of SNPs (single nucleotide polymorphisms), which are more 314 successful for degraded samples (Fabbri et al. 2012). Sample quality, however, can be maximised by using as 315 many hair follicles as possible per sample in the DNA extraction process. Sampling efficiency can also be 316 improved by placing hair tubes on the edge of forest tracks to improve access by surveyors. Given the high rate 317 of error associated with non-invasive genetic sampling, refinement of the process and consideration of 318 environmental conditions associated with each species is paramount to making the process efficient and cost

effective. This study provides guidance for improvements to non-invasive surveys of pine martens in Scotland, 320 and also highlights key areas for assessment prior to surveys of other mammalian species.
